idiom_name: verb method names + named static factory methods (Effective Java item 1)
implementation_notes: Oracle's conventions require method names to be verbs that shorten nothing (`cancel`, `withdraw` - never `setFlag` or `cntusr`), and the first Effective Java item replaces overloaded constructors with named static factories, which is where Java gains most of its intention-revealing power: `BigInteger.probablePrime(bitLength, rnd)` states a contract that `BigInteger(int, int, Random)` could not, and the small vocabulary `from`, `of`, `valueOf`, `instance`/`getInstance`, `newInstance`, `getType` makes call sites predictable. What replaces a documented interface is the pair (signature plus Javadoc `@param`/`@return`/`@throws`) together with `Optional` returns and immutable value types, so absence and mutation are visible in the type. Keep bean-style `getX`/`setX` only where a framework reflects on them (JPA, Jakarta Beans, XML/JSON serializers).
code_sketch:
public final class Order {
    public static Order forCart(CartId cartId, BuyerId buyer) { ... }   // named factory
    public Money total() { ... }                                       // query
    public boolean isCancellable() { ... }                             // predicate
    public void addLine(Sku sku, Quantity quantity) { ... }            // command
    public Optional<CouponCode> appliedCoupon() { ... }                // absence is in the type
}
pitfalls: Bean-style getter/setter pairs hand the caller the representation and scatter invariants; keep them for reflective frameworks and offer model operations (`addLine`) in application code.
`Optional` is a return-type signal only: `Optional<CouponCode> appliedCoupon()` reveals absence, while optional fields, parameters or nested optionals hide it again.

Javadoc is the published contract for callers without the source, so a missing first-sentence summary or an undocumented `@throws` means the promise is unreadable exactly where the pattern is supposed to help.

variants.name: Sealed interfaces and records name the domain alternatives
variants.idiom_name: sealed interface + record cases + exhaustive switch
variants.implementation_notes: From Java 17 the interface itself can name the domain's alternatives: `sealed interface PaymentOutcome permits Approved, Declined, RequiresReview` with record cases tells a caller every legal shape without documentation, and an exhaustive `switch` (no `default`) makes the compiler prove that all of them are handled - a closed, named set of outcomes replaces prose that enumerates what may come back. Records also carry the values with generated, intention-revealing accessors (`outcome.code()` rather than `getCode()`). Use it for results, commands and state machines; keep the open `interface` plus implementations where third parties must be able to add implementations, because sealing closes the hierarchy for good.
pitfalls: Sealing is permanent for the hierarchy: an API that later needs third-party implementations has to reopen the type, which is a source-breaking change.
Records expose their components as accessor methods and structural equality - do not add domain behaviour that depends on hidden state, and never expose mutable collections as record components.
An exhaustive switch still needs a migration plan: adding a new permitted record breaks every consumer's switch at compile time (which is the point) but requires a release-coordinated rollout.
